newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW - Ford CEO bullish on Europe.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Ford CEO bullish on Europe.

text.p: Alex Trotman, chairman and chief executive officer of Ford Motor Co, said on Monday he expected the European car market to rise three percent in 1997 over an estimated 13 to 14 million cars for 1996.
For North America, Ford sees a rise to 15.4 million vehicles, and he expects the Mercosur market in Latin America to grow much faster than America or Europe.

"I see the European market somewhere up there in the high 13-14 (millions). It looks quite good to us, the industry is really doing quite well, with a little bouncing up and down in Britain and a little nervousness in France now that the (government) incentive program is stopped..
"We're still looking for a pretty good industry this year, we're ready to keep rolling," he told Reuters in an interview.
Trotman was in Paris to unveil the Ka, the smallest car in the Ford family, which is being built in Valencia, Spain, with initial volumes of 200,000 per year.

"The reaction to it (Ka) has been so strong that we think that 200,000 will not do it. There is a very urgent study under way right now with component, engines, transmission and assembly to see how high we can get it," Trotman said.
"I don't know whether we can get 240,000 or 250,000 in the first year but that would be the general magnitude, I suspect," he told Reuters.
"It's a new business for Ford, it's the smallest kind of car that we've had in our history in Europe," he said.

Trotman said earlier in an interview with Reuters Financial Television that Britain and Spain were at the moment the cheapest places to build cars in Europe and he added Britain had nearly closed the "quality gap" with Germany.
"Germany is a profitable part of Ford but we do have a cost problem in Germany as a lot of people do. The mark is very strong, the cost of doing business in Germany is very high," he said.

"That is a competitive threat to our German operations and I suspect for many other operations in Germany too. That is something that we are all working on very hard with the full co-operation of our workforce in Germany to address the cost issues."
While Ford's recent European investments were for the Ka in Valencia, Spain, and for the Galaxy in Portugal, Trotman denied investments in these countries were a trend for the company.
"Portugal was very competitive. Valencia happened to work because of the way we were cycling our small cars but I would not call that a trend," he said.
